lessons.title: Probability, Loss and the Learning Objective
objectives: Derive negative log likelihood from conditional probability
Compute a baseline cross-entropy and compare it to perplexity
Diagnose data leakage and measurement traps
lessons.hook: Imagine a system that predicts the next ticket category correctly most of the time but assigns almost zero probability to rare urgent incidents. Accuracy looks healthy, yet its mistakes could be very costly. How should an AI engineer decide what a model has actually learned?
explanation: A language model does not begin with an instruction to produce a sensible paragraph. It learns a probability distribution over possible next tokens given a prefix. If the vocabulary has V symbols, the model produces V real-valued logits, converts them into nonnegative probabilities by softmax, and chooses or samples a token. For token t with logit z_t, the conditional probability is exp(z_t) divided by the sum of exp(z_j) over all vocabulary tokens. Numerically stable implementations subtract the largest logit before taking exponentials. That subtraction changes no probability because the common scaling factor cancels. This connects model architecture to an observable prediction problem.

Suppose a training sequence contains tokens x_1 through x_T. Under an autoregressive factorization, its probability is the product over positions of p(x_t | x_1,...,x_(t-1)). Products of many probabilities become tiny and awkward to optimize, so take the negative natural logarithm. The sequence negative log likelihood is L = -sum_t log p(x_t | preceding tokens). Divide by the number of predicted tokens to obtain mean token loss. If one correct token is assigned probability 0.8, its loss is about 0.223 nats; if assigned probability 0.01, its loss jumps to about 4.605 nats. The loss punishes confident mistakes substantially more than ordinary classification accuracy does.

Cross-entropy follows the same idea when the training target is represented as a one-hot distribution: H(q,p) = -sum_j q_j log p_j, where q has mass one on the observed token. For a dataset with N predictions, the empirical training objective averages these values. The model has no guarantee of understanding meaning simply because this numerical loss decreases; it could memorize patterns, exploit duplicated records or learn correlations that fail on deployment. The evaluation distribution and split design are part of the scientific claim. A lower training loss is not automatically a better real-world AI system.

Perplexity is exp(mean negative log likelihood) when loss uses the natural logarithm. A mean loss of ln(4) corresponds to perplexity 4. Intuitively it resembles the effective number of equally likely alternatives, although real distributions are rarely uniform. Compare perplexities only when tokenization and evaluation data are comparable. Changing the tokenizer changes token boundaries and the number of predictions, so a naive cross-model comparison may mislead. For production systems also separate task utility, latency, calibration, safety, and operating cost from predictive loss.

A reliable experiment starts with a simple baseline. For incident-category prediction, measure a constant-category baseline, a frequency-based probabilistic baseline and a trainable model on the same held-out incidents. Report log loss, class-wise recall, confusion matrix and calibration. Split by time or by incident source when chronological drift or duplicate tickets would make random splitting leak future information. Document data provenance. If model selection repeatedly uses the same test set, that set gradually becomes part of training decisions; preserve an untouched final evaluation split.

The learning objective also determines what the model overlooks. Standard maximum likelihood gives more aggregate weight to patterns that occur often in the training set. A rare but critical security event may contribute little to the average even if missing it has enormous downstream cost. This is why class weighting, risk-sensitive evaluation, human escalation and operational monitoring exist. They are engineering decisions outside the bare next-token likelihood formula. Before modifying the loss, define the target behavior and quantify what errors the system can tolerate.

Consider why choosing the training objective is a model-design decision rather than an afterthought. Negative log-likelihood rewards probability assigned to the observation, not just whether the top-ranked class is correct. A model assigning 0.51 to the observed label receives a much larger loss than one assigning 0.99; this supplies a gradient even for correctly classified examples. The calibration of those probabilities also matters when a downstream decision uses a threshold. Under distribution shift, low training loss cannot establish that probabilities are reliable on deployment data. A useful falsification experiment partitions examples by time or source, checks calibration and out-of-distribution error, and compares against a simple constant predictor. Never choose your final evaluation threshold after repeatedly inspecting a protected test set: that itself turns the test set into a tuning instrument.

examples.title: Hand-computing token loss
examples.walkthrough: A vocabulary contains three possible next words. For the observed token A, a model outputs probabilities A=0.7, B=0.2 and C=0.1. The negative log likelihood is -ln(0.7), approximately 0.357 nats. Now consider an otherwise similar prediction where the model assigns A only 0.02 probability. Its penalty is -ln(0.02), approximately 3.912. The second prediction is more than ten times as costly under log loss. If these are the two predictions in one sequence, the mean is (0.357 + 3.912)/2 = 2.1345. The sequence perplexity is exp(2.1345), approximately 8.45. This illustrates why a high average accuracy cannot hide severe confident errors from cross-entropy.

examples.title: Checking a model against a baseline
examples.walkthrough: An evaluation sample contains ten incident categories: seven are Routine, two are Access and one is Security. A majority-class predictor achieves 70% accuracy by always saying Routine but assigns zero probability to the rare categories, resulting in infinite log loss without smoothing. Apply additive smoothing to produce positive probabilities for each class, then compute average negative log likelihood for the ten actual labels. Compare that to a second predictor assigning a meaningful probability to Security even when it is rare. A reader should see why comparing only accuracy obscures confidence and minority-class quality. Keep both predictors fixed before looking at the test labels.

lessons.title: Optimization, Backpropagation and Generalization
objectives: Derive gradients for a small computational graph and check with finite differences
Implement gradient descent and distinguish training improvement from generalization
lessons.hook: A neural model can fit its training examples and still fail on real inputs. To understand why, we will derive exactly how a loss depends on its weights, implement a gradient check, and then examine what validation performance tells us that training loss cannot.
explanation: Training a model means choosing parameters that reduce a precisely defined loss on observed examples. Start with a prediction z = wx + b and a squared-error objective L = (z - y)^2 / 2 for one observation. The prediction is a function of w and b, so its loss is also a function of both. The derivative with respect to the prediction is dL/dz = z-y; the derivative of z with respect to w is x; therefore the chain rule gives dL/dw = (z-y)x. Likewise dL/db = z-y. This is reverse-mode automatic differentiation in miniature: pass values forward, then propagate local derivatives backward. A neural network's additional layers make the graph larger but do not change the basic rule. Parameter gradients are accumulated contributions from every path through which a parameter influences the output.

For a batch of n examples, mean loss is the sum of per-example losses divided by n. When we minimize that batch mean, the gradient is also the mean of the example gradients. Gradient descent updates a parameter by subtracting learning_rate times its gradient. A learning rate of 0.1 does not imply ten-percent progress: gradient magnitude depends on data scale, current parameters, and loss definition. With a sufficiently large rate, an update may jump across the minimum and increase loss, sometimes diverging. With a very small rate, many iterations may be needed. Momentum keeps a running direction from previous gradients; Adam adjusts per-parameter step sizes using gradient moments. Neither optimizer eliminates the need to inspect the loss curve and evaluate on held-out examples.

The crucial distinction is between optimization and generalization. Optimizing an empirical loss measures fit to the training sample; generalization concerns errors on future examples from the target population. A complex model can memorize noise, leakage or individual examples, giving a low training loss and a much worse validation loss. Regularization, restricted capacity, more representative data, and early stopping can mitigate this; none is a guarantee when the evaluation data are compromised. A validation set guides model choice, whereas the untouched test set estimates performance after the choice has been made. Repeated test-set peeking quietly turns the test set into a second validation set.

Gradient checking detects a different kind of failure: incorrect backpropagation implementation. Replace an analytic derivative at parameter w with a central finite difference [L(w+epsilon)-L(w-epsilon)]/(2 epsilon), using a small perturbation such as 1e-5 in double precision. Compare these, preferably with a relative error scaled to the derivative magnitudes. At very small epsilon, floating-point cancellation dominates; at very large epsilon, truncation error dominates. This check validates derivative code locally, not whether the data or objective make sense. A perfect gradient can optimize the wrong task remarkably efficiently.

To decide whether an optimizer is behaving well, log both gradient norms and parameter-update magnitudes. For the linear example, a parameter update is meaningful only relative to the feature scale and the range of predictions. In deeper networks, exploding gradients can destabilize updates, while vanishing gradients can make early layers learn slowly. Gradient clipping limits the update signal when its norm crosses a threshold, but it changes the dynamics rather than correcting an incorrect architecture. A practical debugging sequence is to overfit a tiny clean batch first, confirm that loss falls, compare analytic and numerical gradients on selected small parameters, then grow the dataset and inspect validation curves. If the tiny batch cannot be fitted, suspect code, labels, or optimization before hyperparameter search. If training succeeds but validation fails, investigate generalization, sampling and leakage before training longer. Neither outcome should be hidden behind a single final accuracy number.

explanation.text:
def loss(w, b, x=2.0, y=5.0):
    return 0.5 * (w*x + b - y)**2

def analytic(w, b, x=2.0, y=5.0):
    error = w*x + b - y
    return error*x, error

def finite_diff(w, b, eps=1e-5):
    return ((loss(w+eps,b)-loss(w-eps,b))/(2*eps),
            (loss(w,b+eps)-loss(w,b-eps))/(2*eps))

w, b = 1.0, 0.0
assert all(abs(u-v) < 1e-6 for u,v in zip(analytic(w,b),finite_diff(w,b)))
gw, gb = analytic(w,b)
w -= 0.1*gw
b -= 0.1*gb
assert abs(loss(w,b)-1.125) < 1e-12
print(w,b,loss(w,b))

explanation: The important operational habit is to trace a failure back to the class of evidence that can actually resolve it. A derivative mismatch requires a gradient test. A loss plateau requires optimization diagnostics. A production mismatch requires representative holdout evaluation and investigation of shifts in incoming data. Do not confuse these diagnoses merely because all three eventually appear as a disappointing performance number.

examples.title: A complete gradient calculation
examples.walkthrough: Use x=2, y=5, w=1 and b=0. The forward pass yields z = 1*2+0 = 2, so the residual is -3 and the half-squared loss is 4.5. Now reverse the graph: dL/dz = -3, dz/dw = 2 and dz/db = 1. Therefore dL/dw = -6 and dL/db = -3. A gradient step with rate 0.1 produces w=1.6 and b=0.3. The new prediction is 3.5 and the new loss is (3.5-5)^2/2 = 1.125. Check both changes, not merely whether a Python script prints a smaller number. The reduction is expected here but does not imply that the same rate is stable for all feature scales or all training samples.

examples.title: Why a gradient check is not a generalization check
examples.walkthrough: Imagine a regression model that includes a unique customer identifier encoded as an enormous lookup table. It can perfectly memorize training targets. Compute its gradients numerically and analytically: both may agree, so the implementation check passes. Yet a new customer identifier offers no meaningful lookup and predictions can be poor. The experiment illustrates two non-interchangeable claims. A gradient check asks whether the derivative of a chosen objective is computed correctly for a chosen input. A held-out evaluation asks whether the resulting model predicts cases it did not train on. Neither answer substitutes for the other. In a production project, check gradients at development time and separately evaluate a representative time-based or entity-disjoint holdout.

lessons.title: Data Splitting and Leakage
objectives: Choose splitting units and chronology that match the deployment prediction task
Detect leakage through preprocessing, duplicate entities and post-outcome features
lessons.hook: Suppose a risk model scores 98 percent accuracy during testing but collapses on the first day of deployment. The culprit may not be the model: its evaluation boundary could allow information from the future, duplicate customers, or target-derived features to cross into training.
explanation: A data split is a claim about which information will be available when the system makes a future prediction. Random rows are only an appropriate splitting unit when observations are sufficiently independent and identically distributed for the intended use. In an employee attrition model, rows from the same employee over multiple months share stable characteristics. If months from one employee appear in training and test, the model can recognize that employee without predicting genuinely unseen people. If deployment predicts new employees, separate by employee identifier. If deployment predicts next quarter for existing employees, separate chronologically and ensure every feature was known at the earlier prediction time. The validation method must simulate the decision that the real system will make.

Leakage occurs whenever information from outside the permitted training boundary influences fitted parameters, preprocessing, labels, or model selection. A vivid example is a feature named termination_completed_at when the prediction target is employee termination in the next ninety days; it is unavailable at scoring time and encodes the outcome. Less obvious leakage arises when a global average, vocabulary, target encoding or imputation statistic is estimated from the entire dataset before the split. Although this step may appear unsupervised, it still carries information from test records into the training pipeline. Fit transformations only on training data and apply the fitted transformation unchanged to validation and test data.

For time series, use an explicit observation cutoff and a prediction horizon. Suppose events through September 30 are available to predict whether an invoice will be late in October. Labels derived from November collections cannot be included in September features, regardless of what timestamps exist in a database export produced in December. Maintain an event_time (when something happened) and availability_time (when your system could have known it). Late-arriving updates make those two distinct. A strict point-in-time feature join respects availability_time as of the prediction timestamp. A gap or embargo around the split boundary may be needed when outcomes span intervals or nearby examples share an event.

Use training data for fitting parameters and preprocessing, validation data for selecting hyperparameters and thresholds, and a reserved test set for the final unbiased estimate. If a team repeatedly looks at test results to decide changes, the test loses its independent role. A low validation loss from a leaked or unrealistic split is not reassurance; inspect data lineage, duplicates and time boundaries before trusting any number. Document the intended deployment population, the sampling unit, class prevalence, missing values, and data drift. Even an impeccable split can fail to represent a new geography or a policy change, so production monitoring remains necessary.

An auditable pipeline makes the split boundary reproducible. Assign every observation a stable row identifier and record the exact exclusion rule, cutoff, label horizon, and feature materialization timestamp. Construct the holdout first, then fit imputation, encoding, vocabulary, scaling and model weights only on the allowed training partition. When tuning, a validation partition can be used repeatedly, but record each candidate and avoid claiming that the best of hundreds of attempts has an unbiased validation score. In time-ordered problems, use a sequence of historical cutoffs, train only before each cutoff, and score a later window, rather than relying on one convenient random shuffle. If training labels take ninety days to mature, do not train using outcomes that would have been unknown at that historical cutoff. Keep a final untouched period for a single evaluation of the selected pipeline. A leakage audit is a data-lineage exercise before it is an algorithm exercise.

explanation.text:
# Minimal split and preprocessing example: no external libraries
rows = [
    {"id": "a", "time": 1, "feature": 1.0},
    {"id": "b", "time": 2, "feature": 2.0},
    {"id": "c", "time": 3, "feature": 3.0},
    {"id": "d", "time": 4, "feature": 4.0},
    {"id": "e", "time": 5, "feature": 100.0},
]
train = [r for r in rows if r["time"] <= 4]
test = [r for r in rows if r["time"] > 4]
mean = sum(r["feature"] for r in train)/len(train)
transformed_test = [r["feature"]-mean for r in test]
assert mean == 2.5
assert transformed_test == [97.5]
print(transformed_test)

explanation: One final trap is training-serving skew: a feature constructed correctly in a historical notebook may be assembled differently by the real-time scoring service. Validate the exact feature definition and availability in both paths, including missing-value handling, entity identifiers, and timezone semantics. A trustworthy offline evaluation must approximate what the live service will know at the instant a decision is made.

examples.title: Spot an outcome-derived feature
examples.walkthrough: An HR dataset contains employee_id, role, months_at_company, resignation_filed_date, and left_within_90_days. The business question is: at the start of each month, who might leave within the following ninety days? resignation_filed_date often becomes known only after a resignation, so including it at an earlier prediction timestamp creates target leakage. Evaluate each feature using a precise availability test: could the scoring service have queried this value at the start-of-month instant? Drop or reconstruct features that fail. If each employee contributes many monthly rows, choose a held-out employee split for new-employee generalization. For next-month prediction on existing employees, prefer a chronological rolling-origin split and validate that features are assembled point-in-time.

examples.title: Why fitting a scaler before splitting is unsafe
examples.walkthrough: Consider four training feature values 1,2,3,4 and one held-out observation 100. If a mean-centering transformer is fitted only on training data, the mean is (1+2+3+4)/4 = 2.5; the transformed test value is 97.5. If preprocessing incorrectly pools all five values first, the mean is 22, and the test value becomes 78. Both are numerically valid transformations, but the latter fitted statistic used the supposedly unseen record. This toy example makes the boundary visible. The difference is not that 97.5 is inherently better than 78; it is that only the training-fitted transformation reproduces the information available at model-training time. Maintain a reproducible pipeline that separately fits and transforms.

lessons.title: Tokenizers and Vocabulary
objectives: Explain why byte, character, word and subword tokenization create different model inputs and costs
Trace BPE merges and distinguish token IDs, UTF-8 bytes and character boundaries
Evaluate domain-specific vocabulary shifts and offset reconstruction failures
lessons.hook: A language model never receives the string you typed as a sequence of meaningful English words. It receives integer IDs selected by a tokenizer. A seemingly harmless tokenizer change can alter context length, retrieval chunk boundaries, multilingual performance, and the behavior of everything trained to consume those IDs. We will construct the mapping rather than treating it as magic.
explanation: A tokenizer establishes a deterministic interface from text to a sequence of discrete symbols. A model commonly consumes token IDs x_1 through x_T rather than raw Unicode text. This interface is not semantically neutral: the representation determines which recurring fragments get short descriptions, how many positions are consumed in the attention context, and how an input can be reconstructed. A word-level vocabulary handles frequent words compactly but suffers badly from unseen words; character units avoid that particular out-of-vocabulary problem while making sequences long. UTF-8 byte tokens can represent any encoded text without an unknown-symbol fallback, at the expense of initially longer sequences. Subword vocabularies seek a middle ground by assigning tokens to frequent fragments, punctuation patterns, and even spaces. A model using subwords may represent common English words as one token, uncommon names as several, and non-English scripts with surprising segmentation. A token is not necessarily a character, syllable, or word.

Byte-pair encoding, or BPE, learns recurring adjacent pairs from a corpus. Consider a toy corpus in which the strings low and lower appear repeatedly. Begin with a specified base alphabet, including an end-of-word marker if the chosen variant uses one. Count adjacent symbol-pair occurrences weighted by training word frequencies, select the most frequent pair, replace it consistently, then recount. A possible first merge is l followed by o into lo, and a later one lo followed by w into low. This description is intentionally specific to a toy BPE variant. Modern production tokenizers differ in their pretokenization rules, byte mappings, reserved token handling, merge ordering, Unicode normalization, and tie-breaking. It would be incorrect to infer a deployed tokenizer’s token count from an English-language rule of thumb.

A tokenizer must specify both encoding and decoding conventions. The token integer 42 has no intrinsic meaning; it identifies an entry in a particular versioned vocabulary. Moving from one vocabulary to another changes the interpretation of embedding-table rows, so swapping tokenizers under a trained model is not a harmless preprocessing tweak. Special tokens also need a protected namespace. A start token, an end-of-sequence marker, a tool boundary marker and a literal user string that merely resembles a marker must not collapse to the same control signal. In a chat system, the conversation template and its reserved tokens shape the serialized input in addition to the visible message text. Treat these as part of an immutable model contract, alongside model weights and normalization rules.

Unicode creates practical traps. A grapheme visible as one character can contain multiple Unicode code points; each code point may occupy multiple bytes in UTF-8. Combining accents, emoji variation selectors, and zero-width joiners mean a naive assumption of one visible character per code point is false. Offsets from the tokenizer might refer to byte positions or code-point indices; a browser selection or annotation may use yet another coordinate system. For example, the accented letter é can be written as the single code point U+00E9 or as e followed by combining acute U+0301. These strings look similar but have different UTF-8 bytes unless normalization is applied. When building citation spans and document extractors, store original text, the normalization policy and an explicit offset mapping. Otherwise a highlight may drift by multiple characters on multilingual documents.

Vocabulary selection is a distributional engineering decision, not simply a compression contest. If a tokenizer is trained mostly on ordinary English, medical terminology, source code, or South Asian languages may consume disproportionately many tokens. Longer segmentation increases inference positions and can change where truncation happens. Yet making a very large vocabulary has costs: the embedding and output projection parameters grow with vocabulary size, while rare tokens may have inadequate training data. One useful measurement is tokens per input byte by language and domain, measured on a representative, consented evaluation corpus. A second is whether exact text can be reconstructed after encode/decode. A third is how stable important entity boundaries are under tokenization, even though model quality cannot be inferred from token compression alone.

In production, persist the tokenizer version with all prepared training and embedding datasets. A change in Unicode normalization, pretokenizer regex, BPE merge table, or special-token policy can invalidate cached encoded documents. Never conflate word counts with billable token counts: every provider has its own tokenizer and message serialization overhead. Test adversarial strings including mixed scripts, control-like text, whitespace, long numbers, mathematical notation, emoji sequences, and unusual file paths. Before a model deployment, check both segmentation statistics and application-level behavior on those cases. Tokenization is the first component of the model’s input semantics, and bugs here can masquerade as retrieval, prompting, or context-window failures.

examples.title: Manual BPE merge counts
examples.walkthrough: Take frequencies low: five and lower: two, and initially split each word into code-point characters. Pair l-o appears seven times, o-w appears seven times, w-e appears twice, and e-r appears twice. Because the two top counts tie, our demonstration code deliberately breaks ties alphabetically, selecting (l,o) first. After replacement the sequences are (lo,w) and (lo,w,e,r), so the pair (lo,w) occurs seven times. Merge this next to obtain the symbol low. Notice what is *not* implied: lower has not necessarily become one token; its remaining e and r still require additional merges. This exercise proves the training counts under the declared toy algorithm only. Different pretokenization or tie-breaking can produce different merge tables even for the same text.

examples.title: Unicode offsets in multilingual highlighting
examples.walkthrough: Compare s1 as café using precomposed é with s2 as cafe followed by U+0301 combining acute. The rendered words may be visually identical. Yet a UTF-8 encoded representation of the accented part has different byte boundaries, and a character-count offset need not equal a byte-count offset. Suppose a citation system stores the start of the final visible letter as byte index three and later interprets that number as a Unicode code-point offset into normalized text. Some examples seem to work until mixed scripts or emoji precede the span. The safe solution is to record original bytes, normalized text, and a checked mapping of source offsets to display offsets. A model answering a question about the document cannot repair a corrupted highlight mapping.

lessons.title: Embeddings and Vector Geometry
objectives: Derive dot-product and cosine similarity and identify the role of vector norms
Explain why trained embedding proximity does not prove factual equivalence or causality
Implement and validate a small exact nearest-neighbor baseline with normalized vectors
lessons.hook: An embedding database often advertises that close vectors mean similar ideas. That statement is only a hypothesis tied to training objectives, representation choices and evaluation data. To design a trustworthy retrieval system, we need to calculate the geometry, separate semantic relevance from vector distance, and make a numerical example that can fail for the right reasons.
explanation: A learned embedding associates an input unit with a vector in R^d, where d is the chosen representation dimension. In a token embedding layer, the model gathers a row of a learned matrix E with shape V by d for each token ID. Those rows are parameters adjusted by training; they are not dictionary definitions. A text-embedding encoder instead computes a single vector from an entire sequence, possibly by pooling internal states or using a trained projection. Two systems can both output 768-dimensional vectors and still encode incompatible geometries because dimensions acquire meaning jointly with the model objective and data. Thus an embedding index must retain its model identifier, version, preprocessing specification and any normalization policy; dimension alone is never an interoperability guarantee.

The dot product a·b is the sum over coordinates a_i b_i. Euclidean distance between a and b is the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences. Cosine similarity divides the dot product by ||a|| ||b||, measuring alignment rather than magnitude, provided both norms are nonzero. If vectors are L2-normalized to unit length, their dot product equals cosine similarity. Moreover, squared Euclidean distance for unit vectors is ||a-b||² = 2-2(a·b); maximizing cosine is therefore equivalent to minimizing Euclidean distance on the unit sphere. This equivalence does not hold unchanged for arbitrary unnormalized vectors. Models may encode confidence or document properties in vector norms, so normalization can change ranking and must be an explicit, validated decision.

For a worked example take query q=(1,1), candidate A=(2,0), and candidate B=(0.8,0.8). Dot products are q·A=2 and q·B=1.6, so raw dot-product retrieval prefers A. Norms give ||q||=sqrt(2), ||A||=2, ||B||=sqrt(1.28), so cosine(q,A)=1/sqrt(2), approximately 0.7071, while cosine(q,B)=1. Cosine retrieval prefers B because it aligns perfectly with the query direction. Neither answer can be declared the relevant one without a task-specific relevance judgment. When you implement retrieval, label the distance convention used by the index and verify that the client, index builder and evaluation code apply the same convention.

Vector search is an approximation of a semantic matching task, not semantic truth. An encoder optimized to make paraphrases close might be weak on numerical consistency, legal negation, or rare product codes. Queries such as the policy permits access and the policy denies access may share most surface words while expressing opposite requirements. A top similarity score does not demonstrate that a cited document entails the generated answer. Retrieval evaluation should measure recall at k, mean reciprocal rank, or nDCG against independently labeled query-document judgments, then test how those metrics change across domains, languages and document age. Grounded answer evaluation is a separate downstream requirement because a generator may still hallucinate after good retrieval.

An exact brute-force nearest-neighbor baseline is valuable before introducing an approximate index. With N vectors of dimension d, computing all query dot products costs roughly O(Nd), and storing float32 vectors needs approximately 4Nd bytes before index overhead and metadata. Approximate nearest-neighbor structures reduce query cost for large N but introduce recall-latency-memory trade-offs. First compare every approximate result against exact top-k rankings on a held-out query set; then quantify recall@k and latency under concurrency. Preserve deterministic tie-breaking for reproducibility, and decide how to handle zero vectors, NaNs, duplicates and missing embeddings. Beware of a subtle evaluation leak: if the reference exact baseline itself applies the wrong normalization rule, the approximate index can look perfect while returning the wrong ranking for the application.

Embedding quality also depends on chunking and context. If a policy paragraph is split in the middle of a negation exception, its vector may omit the condition needed to answer accurately. If chunks are so large that unrelated topics are mixed, a single pooled embedding can obscure a narrow fact. Chunk overlap can protect continuity but creates duplicates and amplifies retrieval of repeated boilerplate. A robust RAG system stores source IDs and character offsets with each chunk, deduplicates near-identical hits, and can reconstruct the cited passage. A knowledge graph can supplement vector search by encoding entities, temporal validity and explicit relationships; it does not magically eliminate embedding errors. The engineering question is whether your measured retrieval failures are due to representation, segmentation, indexing or the downstream answerer.

Normalize the comparison: q has length sqrt(2); A has length 2; B has length sqrt(.8²+.8²), or sqrt(1.28). Cosine for A is 2/(2 sqrt(2))≈0.7071, but for B it is 1 because B points in exactly the query direction. Both calculations are mathematically correct, but they encode different ranking priorities. This is why a production index and query client must agree about normalization. To choose a metric for a product, compare measured relevance rather than visual intuition about vector arrows.

examples.title: Memory and exact-search accounting
examples.walkthrough: Suppose you index one million documents with 768-dimensional float32 embeddings. The raw vector payload is 1,000,000 × 768 × 4 = 3,072,000,000 bytes, approximately 3.072 decimal gigabytes or 2.861 GiB. This excludes source text, metadata, HNSW links, replicas and operating-system overhead. An exact single-query dot-product scan performs on the order of 768 million multiply-add contributions. An approximate index might return a smaller shortlist faster, but you must establish its recall@10 against an exact reference under the same similarity definition. Measure both end-to-end latency and retrieval correctness; fitting vectors in RAM does not by itself guarantee query throughput under concurrent traffic.

lessons.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
objectives: Derive QK transpose scaling and output shapes
Implement row-wise causal softmax safely
Explain mask and precision failure modes
lessons.hook: The attention operation is often presented as one line of matrix algebra, yet production bugs hide in its shapes, masks, and normalization. We will build a numerical attention head from first principles, prove what the weights mean, and test a deliberately masked input whose future tokens must never influence an earlier prediction.
explanation: Let token representations be X with shape (T,d_model), and let learned projections W_Q, W_K and W_V produce Q of shape (T,d_k), K of shape (T,d_k), and V of shape (T,d_v). The matrix QK^T contains one compatibility score per ordered pair of query and key positions: shape (T,T). Multiplying its row-softmax weights by V yields an output (T,d_v). Each row of attention weights sums to one on allowed positions, but that does not mean weights directly encode human-readable explanations of a model decision. They represent one computational routing stage that downstream layers can transform or ignore. For minibatches and heads, keep batch and head dimensions explicit rather than assuming a single matrix.

Scale dot products by 1/sqrt(d_k). If unscaled independent query and key coordinates have zero mean and unit variance, their sum of d_k products has variance roughly d_k under simplifying assumptions. Large logit magnitudes push softmax toward saturation and can make derivatives small. Scaling makes logit spread less sensitive to key dimension, although trained representations will not satisfy independent unit-variance assumptions exactly. Softmax must be computed over the KEY axis separately for each query; normalizing columns instead changes the operation. For numerical stability, subtract the maximum permitted score in each row before exponentiation; this preserves probabilities algebraically.

Autoregressive training applies a causal mask M where M_ij is zero if key j is visible to query i and negative infinity otherwise. The first query sees only the first key; the third query sees the first three. In a full training forward pass, causal masking allows parallel evaluation of all positions without leaking later token content. Padding masks are a separate concern: they prevent aggregation from positions that only serve to equalize batch lengths. A common error is to mask the query dimension rather than key positions. Another is to feed a row in which every key is masked into naïve softmax, producing undefined 0/0 after shifting negative infinities. Define explicit behavior or exclude invalid queries.

Consider one query q=(1,0) and two keys k1=(1,0), k2=(0,1), with d_k=2. The scaled logits are 1/sqrt(2) and zero; their exponentials are about 2.028 and 1. Thus the first weight is about 0.670 and second about 0.330. If corresponding values are v1=(2,0) and v2=(0,4), the output is approximately (1.340,1.320). This weighted value sum is not itself a selected token; it is a continuous representation. A sharp distribution can approximate selection, while a diffuse one blends many value vectors. Changing values without changing keys changes the mixture but not the attention probabilities.

Attention is quadratic in sequence length for the explicit score matrix: T by T per head, though optimized kernels avoid materializing that entire matrix and exploit IO-efficient tiling. Computational cost and memory cost are not the same metric. A naïve implementation using NumPy is ideal for auditing semantics but is not the recommended high-throughput production implementation. Verify masks with counterfactual testing: change only future input tokens and assert earlier causal outputs remain unchanged. Verify softmax row sums and all-finite outputs using multiple shapes. These tests catch wrong axes and accidental future leakage more effectively than a single happy-path numerical example.

For reproducible debugging, compare an optimized implementation against a plain reference on the same inputs and masks. Record both the dtype and the numerical tolerance; floating-point operation order can change results slightly without violating the attention contract. Test gradients separately, because matching forward outputs does not establish correct backward propagation through masking and softmax.

Finally, keep causal self-attention distinct from encoder bidirectional attention and cross-attention. In a bidirectional encoder, a query may use both earlier and later keys. In cross-attention, queries and keys can have different sequence lengths, producing a rectangular compatibility matrix. A mask is therefore a policy on allowed query-key pairs, not an inherent property of softmax. The same algebra serves different modeling problems, and shape assertions should reflect the selected mechanism rather than blindly demand square matrices.

explanation.text:
import numpy as np

def attention(q, k, v, causal=False):
    q, k, v = map(lambda z: np.asarray(z, dtype=np.float64), (q, k, v))
    assert q.ndim == k.ndim == v.ndim == 2
    assert q.shape[1] == k.shape[1] and k.shape[0] == v.shape[0]
    logits = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(q.shape[1])
    if causal:
        assert q.shape[0] == k.shape[0]
        logits = np.where(np.tril(np.ones(logits.shape, dtype=bool)), logits, -np.inf)
    logits -= logits.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    weights = np.exp(logits)
    weights /= weights.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return weights @ v, weights

q=np.array([[1.,0.],[0.,1.],[1.,1.]])
v=np.array([[2.,0.],[0.,4.],[1.,3.]])
out,w=attention(q,q,v,causal=True)
assert np.allclose(w.sum(axis=1),1)
assert np.allclose(np.triu(w,1),0)
changed=q.copy(); changed[-1]=[50.,-10.]
out2,_=attention(changed,changed,v,causal=True)
assert np.allclose(out[:2],out2[:2])
print('causal invariance PASS',w)

Multiply the first value vector (2,0) by that weight, and the second (0,4) by the complement. The final representation is about (1.340,1.320). If the raw logits had been normalized along a different axis, the probabilities would not describe a distribution over keys for this query. The final row may depend on every position, but earlier rows are barred from seeing the future. Importantly, test with changed keys AND changed values: modifying only the query can accidentally miss a future-value leakage bug. This is stronger than checking that a numerical matrix happens to be lower triangular.

lessons.title: Positional Information and Multi-Head Attention
objectives: Explain permutation symmetry of attention without position
Trace positional representations and head shapes
Identify why multiple heads do not guarantee different learned roles
lessons.hook: Imagine shuffling the words of a sentence while keeping the same token vectors. A bare self-attention layer without position information cannot tell which arrangement came first. To engineer sequence models, we need an explicit representation of order, plus a disciplined way to split, route, and recombine multiple attention heads.
explanation: Bare self-attention computed from token embeddings is permutation equivariant: if P is a permutation matrix reordering tokens, replacing X with PX reorders Q, K, and V consistently, so attention(PX) = P attention(X) when no order-sensitive mask is applied. Permutation equivariance is not position awareness. A language task such as distinguishing “dog bites man” from “man bites dog” cannot rely solely on an unordered bag of token identities. Positional information breaks this ambiguity by providing a signal connected to token index or relative distance. A causal mask also introduces an order-dependent visibility relation, but it is not a complete substitute for all positional information in typical language-model designs.

One classic solution adds a positional encoding vector p_i to the token embedding x_i before projection. In the original Transformer, a sinusoidal encoding assigns alternating sine and cosine channels at different frequencies. For even channel index 2j, PE(i,2j)=sin(i/10000^(2j/d_model)); for odd channel 2j+1, PE(i,2j+1)=cos(i/10000^(2j/d_model)). These formulas require treating j as a zero-based frequency pair index; the exponent is not based on the absolute channel index twice. The resulting representation uses a combination of slow and fast positional variation. Different approaches learn absolute positions, add pairwise relative biases to logits, or rotate Q and K based on positions. They differ in extrapolation behavior and invariances, so do not equate their names.

Multi-head attention performs several scaled dot-product operations in parallel. For H heads with equal head dimension d_h, the common choice d_model = H*d_h makes concatenating per-head outputs restore model width before an output projection W_O. For a batch B and time T, Q often has shape (B,H,T,d_h), K the same shape, and V typically (B,H,T,d_vh). The attention weights then have shape (B,H,T,T), not simply (T,T). Splitting a flattened projection into heads is a reshape and transpose with an exact memory-layout contract. Accidentally swapping T and H can produce shape-compatible code for some sizes while mixing tokens across heads.

An example with d_model=8 and H=2 yields two heads of width four. Suppose both heads receive a sequence of three tokens. Each produces a 3 by 4 output matrix; concatenating the last dimensions yields a 3 by 8 representation. An output matrix of shape 8 by 8 then mixes information across head channels. This projection is important because heads can develop different subspace features, yet head labels have no fixed semantic identity. One cannot promise that head zero will always track syntax and head one will always track factual references. Models can learn redundant or weak heads, and head pruning often has surprisingly task-dependent effects.

Positional encodings interact with context extension. Learned absolute position tables can fail for positions never trained, unless embeddings are extrapolated or expanded with care. Sinusoids are defined for any index but being mathematically defined does not guarantee a network performs reliably far beyond training lengths. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) encode relative displacement in dot products through paired rotations of Q and K, but practical long-context behavior also depends on the frequency spectrum and training. Relative-position biases can add explicit preferences for nearby positions. Always evaluate position interpolation and longer contexts empirically rather than assuming an analytic construction solves generalization.

In code review, adversarially test reordering. Remove positional signals from an unmasked attention implementation and verify that permuting tokens merely permutes outputs. Then add absolute positional vectors, reorder only token content while holding positions fixed, and observe that the equality generally no longer holds. This pair of tests distinguishes the mathematical symmetry from a model-accuracy question. Separately, inspect head reshaping with non-square tensors such as B=2, H=3, T=5, d_h=4; such choices expose accidental dimension coincidences. The teaching objective is a rigorous mental model for order, not a catalog of positional buzzwords.

explanation.text:
import numpy as np

def pos_encoding(length, width):
    assert width % 2 == 0
    pos=np.arange(length, dtype=float)[:,None]
    pair=np.arange(width//2, dtype=float)[None,:]
    angle=pos/(10000**(2*pair/width))
    out=np.empty((length,width))
    out[:,0::2]=np.sin(angle)
    out[:,1::2]=np.cos(angle)
    return out

def head_split(x,heads):
    batch,time,width=x.shape
    assert width%heads==0
    return x.reshape(batch,time,heads,width//heads).transpose(0,2,1,3)

p=pos_encoding(5,8)
assert np.allclose(p[0,0::2],0)
assert np.allclose(p[0,1::2],1)
x=np.arange(2*5*12).reshape(2,5,12)
y=head_split(x,3)
assert y.shape==(2,3,5,4)
assert np.array_equal(y.transpose(0,2,1,3).reshape(x.shape),x)
print('position and head layout PASS')

At position one the vector is approximately (0.84147,0.54030,0.01000,0.99995). These values are added to the token embeddings in the original architecture; they are not probabilities and should not be normalized by softmax. The transpose is vital: head becomes its own axis before time, so a separate head can attend along the five-position dimension. To invert the bookkeeping, transpose back to (2,5,3,4) and reshape to (2,5,12). A round-trip identity assertion verifies that the operation did not lose or reorder values. This assertion does not prove attention semantics, but it isolates one easy-to-overlook tensor layout bug.

lessons.title: KV Caching
objectives: Trace why autoregressive generation can reuse old keys and values
Calculate cache memory in bytes and distinguish GQA from MHA
Detect cache position and stale-state failures
lessons.hook: Generating one token at a time appears to call attention on nearly the same prefix repeatedly. Why recompute the representations of all earlier positions if those past values do not change in a causal transformer? KV caching exploits that observation, but only if we get positions, ownership and attention masks exactly right.
explanation: An autoregressive decoder predicts the next token conditioned on a prefix. During initial prefill it processes a prompt and computes the key and value tensors at every layer. At generation step t, only the newest token needs new key and value entries, because the attention representations of earlier positions cannot depend on unseen future tokens under causal masking. The latest query compares itself against the cached key sequence, obtains weights over the entire visible history, and forms a weighted sum of cached values. Cached entries are not model outputs or hidden-state snapshots in a generic sense; they are specifically keys and values for each layer in the transformer stack.

For standard multi-head attention, memory scales as 2 * layers * batch * sequence_length * number_of_KV_heads * head_dim * bytes_per_element. The factor two counts keys and values; it does not count queries, which are transient for the active step. For example, with 24 layers, batch 1, 4096 cached positions, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128 and two bytes per element, memory is 2*24*1*4096*8*128*2 = 402,653,184 bytes, or exactly 384 MiB. The same formula yields more than double this memory when sequence length or concurrent requests grows. Allocate for peak concurrency and fragmentation, not only a single user request.

Grouped-query attention, or GQA, reduces cache memory because several query heads share each KV head. If a model has 32 query heads but 8 KV heads, there are four query heads per KV group, and the stored KV tensor has eight head slots rather than thirty-two. Multi-query attention is the extreme case with one shared key head and one value head per layer. These changes alter model representation and computational behavior; it is incorrect to replace an existing trained standard-MHA model with GQA by only changing the inference cache shape. Cache layouts must match the architecture and the projection weights used by that model.

Caching improves compute efficiency, but it does not make generation constant-time with respect to context. Each new query still attends across up to t cached key positions. As t grows, per-token attention work and memory reads can rise even though recomputation of earlier key/value projections is avoided. Real throughput depends on prefill versus decode workloads, batch scheduling, memory bandwidth, kernel choices and cache allocation. This is why measuring a single-token latency on a short prompt cannot predict server performance for multiple long conversations. Distinguish time to first token from steady-state tokens per second.

Cache validity depends on exact token identities, positions, model weights and the context serialization policy. If a prompt changes midway, the old cache cannot generally be reused as though it were computed for the new sequence. In a decoder with rotary position embeddings, newly generated tokens must use the correct absolute position when constructing Q and K rotations; reusing position zero for each generated token gives different results from full recomputation. When sliding-window or paged attention is used, logical positions and physical memory slots must be decoupled. A memory slot reused for a different request must never expose residual keys from the previous user.

An adversarial correctness test compares full-prefix recomputation with incremental cache decoding on a small deterministic model. Feed tokens one at a time, append their keys and values, and compare each newest-token output to the last output row from full causal attention on the entire prefix. These should match within numeric tolerance if the positional and masking semantics are consistent. Randomly modify an earlier token and ensure that cache invalidation or prefix-rebuild logic responds correctly. For a multi-tenant server, also test session isolation and rollback after cancelled or failed generations. Speed optimizations are only trustworthy when their mathematical contract survives these perturbations.

explanation.text:
import numpy as np

def newest_full(q,k,v):
    logits=q[-1:]@k.T/np.sqrt(q.shape[-1])
    w=np.exp(logits-logits.max(axis=1,keepdims=True))
    return (w/w.sum(axis=1,keepdims=True))@v

def incremental(q_steps,k_steps,v_steps):
    cache_k=[];cache_v=[];outputs=[]
    for q,k,v in zip(q_steps,k_steps,v_steps):
        cache_k.append(k);cache_v.append(v)
        all_k=np.stack(cache_k);all_v=np.stack(cache_v)
        outputs.append(newest_full(np.stack([q]),all_k,all_v)[0])
    return np.stack(outputs)

rng=np.random.default_rng(7)
q=rng.normal(size=(6,4)); k=rng.normal(size=(6,4));v=rng.normal(size=(6,3))
out=incremental(q,k,v)
for t in range(1,len(q)+1):
    expected=newest_full(q[:t],k[:t],v[:t])[0]
    assert np.allclose(out[t-1],expected,atol=1e-12)
bytes_used=2*24*1*4096*8*128*2
assert bytes_used==402653184
print('cache equivalence PASS; MiB=',bytes_used/2**20)

lessons.title: Data Pipelines and Deduplication
objectives: Design a reproducible, leakage-resistant pretraining data pipeline with provenance and shard-level manifests
Distinguish exact hashing from approximate near-duplicate detection and quantify false positives
Implement a deterministic document-level MinHash-style similarity experiment and verify deduplication ordering
lessons.hook: Imagine your trillion-token training run finishes on time, yet its evaluation score collapses when the benchmark is rewritten. A subtle cause may be upstream: duplicated web pages, benchmark answers copied into training data, or sample-specific normalization applied after splitting. Efficient accelerator kernels cannot rescue a corrupted data contract. This lesson turns raw text into auditable training examples.
explanation: A language-model dataset is not merely a directory of scraped files. It is a versioned transformation from raw documents to a sequence of training tokens with explicit inclusion criteria. A rigorous pipeline starts with immutable raw objects and source identifiers. It then applies licensing and use-policy screening, basic quality and language filters, personally identifiable information handling, decontamination against evaluation sets, near-duplicate control, and finally a pinned tokenizer and packing policy. Record the order: changing the order changes which information survives and what is counted. For example, filtering exact duplicates after tokenization may catch identical token streams but can waste substantial preprocessing effort; hashing canonicalized document text earlier can remove boilerplate cheaply. A stable document identifier must survive transformations so that exclusion decisions can be audited. When the raw corpus changes, treat the resulting dataset as a new artifact, not the same dataset with a new filename.

Exact deduplication typically computes a cryptographic digest of canonicalized bytes. Under a chosen canonicalization, digest equality is evidence of identical strings, not of semantic equivalence. Unicode normalization, case folding, whitespace collapsing, and punctuation stripping are policy decisions: they may remove noise, but they can erase distinctions in code, mathematics, and multilingual writing. Near-duplicate detection uses signatures that approximate text overlap. For shingle sets A and B, Jaccard similarity is |A intersection B| / |A union B|. MinHash exploits the property that, under a uniform random permutation over the shingle universe, the probability that two sets have the same minimum is their Jaccard similarity. With k approximately independent hash functions, the fraction of matching minima estimates that probability with standard error roughly sqrt(J(1-J)/k). Locality-sensitive hashing can retrieve candidates, but every candidate policy still needs an explicit threshold and a false-positive audit. Similarity is not plagiarism detection, and a short boilerplate sentence shared by different documents is not proof that either should be dropped.

The unit of splitting matters as much as the deduplication algorithm. If a document is chunked into overlapping windows before a train/validation split, nearly identical windows can fall on both sides and inflate metrics. Partition by source entity, document family, or a defensible temporal boundary before constructing chunks. Decontaminate held-out evaluation prompts against the complete candidate training corpus, including paraphrased and template variants where feasible. Keep a testable manifest per shard: source revision, filtering rules, tokenizer checksum, token count, document count, random seed, dedup threshold, exclusion counts by reason, and a checksum of the output shard. If a trainer reports unexpectedly high throughput after a data change, check whether it silently skipped short documents or stopped on failed shards; tokens consumed must agree with manifest totals, not merely with loader iteration counts.

For statistical reasoning, do not mistake a reduced dataset size for proof of improved generalization. Dedup can make sampling fairer and reduce memorization, but overly aggressive filtering may disproportionately remove rare languages, repeated legal expressions, or minority dialects. Audit retained distributions and evaluate downstream accuracy, calibration, contamination and memorization across groups. A reproducible pipeline makes each choice explicit: which sources were excluded, why the policy is justified, and how one would roll it back. This differs from a dashboard that only reports 'duplicates removed': auditability requires that a reviewer can reconstruct which records changed and can demonstrate whether an evaluation document could have leaked across boundaries. As a practical training design, version manifests and pin deterministic seeds so identical input plus configuration reproduces the same ordered sequence of tokenized shards.

A defensible engineering write-up should also include a falsification plan. Record one measured observation, one estimated quantity, and one clearly stated assumption. Change one assumption at a time and test whether the design decision reverses. If the outcome changes materially under realistic alternatives, the plan requires a sensitivity range rather than a single headline figure. Run the included test under a clean Python interpreter and retain the output, including the exact source revision used for the estimate. This makes performance and quality claims independently reproducible.

examples.title: Exact versus near-duplicate on a small corpus
examples.walkthrough: Take document A as "the river runs beside the old bridge", B as "the river runs beside the stone bridge", and C as A with repeated spaces. Whitespace-canonicalize A and C; a SHA-256 digest then matches them exactly. A and B do not hash to the same digest. With word bigrams, A has six shingles and B has six. Their common shingles are "the river", "river runs", "runs beside", "beside the", four in all; the union has eight. Jaccard similarity is therefore 4/8=0.5. At a policy threshold of 0.8, A and B are deliberately retained. A system that conflates exact equivalence and topical similarity could delete B. To confirm this, calculate the sets explicitly, compare all pairwise scores, and inspect the output rather than trusting the number of retained documents alone.

lessons.title: Training Resource Accounting
objectives: Estimate training FLOPs with a defensible approximation and explain omitted terms
Compute Adam mixed-precision training-state memory and sharding tradeoffs
Separate theoretical compute, effective throughput, wall-clock and end-to-end cost
lessons.hook: A proposed 7-billion-parameter run appears to fit a GPU according to an optimistic spreadsheet, but the first optimizer step triggers an out-of-memory error. The missing quantities were not mystery overhead: optimizer moments, gradients, activations and communication buffers were simply omitted. Training resource accounting is a falsifiable engineering budget, not a parameter-count slogan.
explanation: Pretraining resource estimates begin with a model and token budget. A widely used dense-transformer approximation is training FLOPs C approximately 6 N D, where N is the number of non-embedding or trainable parameters according to the chosen convention and D is the number of training tokens. The factor six is a back-of-envelope convention: a forward matrix multiply costs roughly two operations per multiply-accumulate, and backward propagation is on the order of twice forward for the same large matrix operations. Attention at long context, vocabulary projections, embedding tables, recomputation, sparsity, optimizer kernels and padding make the real count differ. Record the counting convention; an estimate that silently uses 7 billion parameters in one row and 6.7 billion non-embedding parameters in another cannot be audited. FLOPs are an estimate of *work*, not seconds and not money.

For N=7 billion and D=100 billion, C=6*(7e9)*(100e9)=4.2e21 floating point operations. Suppose eight accelerators each sustain 100 teraFLOP/s on the actual training workload, not their advertised peak. Their combined effective rate is 8e14 FLOP/s. Idealized compute time is 4.2e21 / 8e14 = 5.25e6 seconds, about 60.8 days. This is already optimistic because the sustained-throughput assumption must include the communication and recomputation characteristics of the actual job. A 60 percent model-FLOP utilization measurement relative to suitable theoretical peak could yield a different sustained rate; do not apply the same utilization penalty twice. For any plan, measure achieved tokens per second on a representative microbenchmark and compare estimated delivered FLOPs per second against peak to expose the implied utilization.

GPU capacity often fails before raw FLOP capacity. Consider a common mixed-precision Adam arrangement with 2 bytes per low-precision model parameter, 2 bytes per low-precision gradient, 4 bytes per FP32 master parameter, and 8 bytes for Adam first and second FP32 moments: 16 bytes per parameter. Thus 7e9 parameters require approximately 112 GB of persistent states under this specific implementation, before activation storage, temporary workspace, communication buffers and fragmentation. Some frameworks maintain FP32 gradients, fused states, or BF16 moments instead, so this number is a *specified configuration*, not universal physics. With eight data-parallel devices, naïve replication uses that full state budget per device. ZeRO-1 partitions optimizer states, ZeRO-2 partitions gradients as well, and ZeRO-3 partitions model parameters too, with communication and runtime tradeoffs. An idealized equal partition of all 112 GB is 14 GB per device; actual peak must also budget all-gather buffers, activations and uneven shard placement.

Batching and sequence length affect memory and time even at fixed token count. Global token batch is microbatch_per_device times sequence_length times gradient_accumulation_steps times data_parallel_workers, provided each sample is fully packed and masks are appropriate. Increasing accumulation does not automatically reduce total training FLOPs, although it can trade throughput for peak activation memory. Activation checkpointing recomputes intermediate forward activations during backpropagation to reduce memory at the cost of additional operations. Padding wastes attention operations and changes effective tokens-per-step; a billing plan must distinguish processed padded tokens from useful loss-bearing tokens. Finally, convert compute duration into cost only after accounting for queue time, setup, failures, checkpoint writes, storage, network and realistic accelerator availability. A strong estimate reports ranges and sensitivity rather than a single misleadingly precise number.

Activation memory depends on implementation details that the simple sixteen-bytes-per-parameter optimizer estimate deliberately omits. A transformer retains or recomputes intermediate tensors needed for backward propagation. Sequence length, attention implementation, model width, layer count and microbatch size change activation pressure even when model parameter count is fixed. Activation checkpointing can reduce saved tensors but invokes extra forward recomputation. Attention kernels that avoid materializing a full quadratic attention matrix change memory scaling; nonetheless long contexts still increase compute and working-set pressure. In capacity planning, measure actual peak allocated and reserved bytes under representative sequence-length distributions rather than assuming that idle memory after parameter sharding is usable for activations.

Distributed training also incurs communication: a sharded optimizer must reconstruct or stream the parameter fragments needed for each layer, reduce or scatter gradients, and synchronize at stages chosen by the parallelism strategy. Interconnect bandwidth and collective latency can dominate small microbatches, and pipeline or tensor parallelism introduces further transfers. A theoretical FLOP budget estimates arithmetic work, not communication stalls, data-loader idle time, failed jobs, checkpoint serialization or slowest-rank stragglers. Record observed tokens per second, utilization and step-time percentiles; use those measures to forecast calendar duration with a retry margin. ZeRO-3 can make persistent model state fit while still failing at the first backward step due to activation or all-gather peaks. The governing test is a profiled full training step, not merely a parameter-memory spreadsheet.

A per-device 80 GB card cannot hold 112 GB of replicated mixed-precision Adam persistent state, never mind activations. At an idealized ZeRO-3 eight-way shard, 112/8=14 GB of persistent state per device, but memory reserved for all-gather, activations and other components still must be quantified. examples.title: Executable optimizer-state and throughput calculator

walkthrough.text: This small calculator intentionally requires the precision policy and device rate to be stated. It reports both replicated and perfectly sharded persistent state memory in decimal GB; GPU vendor labels may use different units. Assertions protect the numerical estimates and demonstrate that halving measured sustained throughput doubles idealized compute time. For real capacity planning compare these results with profiler-measured peak allocations and observed training step times rather than projecting peak silicon TFLOPs. Treat this estimator as a lower-bound accounting exercise, not a hardware benchmark. Recalculate for measured sustained throughput, then separately estimate activation peaks and collective communication, because parameter sharding alone does not make the step executable. Test a throughput-halving scenario and a microbatch-doubling scenario: the former changes compute time, while the latter changes activation pressure. Keep the program assertions as checks on arithmetic and units, and validate the resulting capacity plan with a profiler trace before committing to an accelerator purchase.

def training_budget(params, tokens, devices, device_tflops, bytes_per_param=16):
    assert params > 0 and tokens > 0 and devices > 0 and device_tflops > 0
    flops = 6 * params * tokens
    seconds = flops / (devices * device_tflops * 1e12)
    replicated_gb = params * bytes_per_param / 1e9
    sharded_gb = replicated_gb / devices
    return flops, seconds, replicated_gb, sharded_gb

f, t, replicated, sharded = training_budget(7e9, 1e11, 8, 100)
assert f == 4.2e21
assert abs(t - 5.25e6) < 1e-6
assert replicated == 112 and sharded == 14
_, slower, _, _ = training_budget(7e9, 1e11, 8, 50)
assert slower == 2*t
print('FLOPs:', f, 'days:', round(t/86400, 2),
      'replicated GB:', replicated, 'sharded GB:', sharded)

lessons.title: Batching and Latency
objectives: Distinguish prompt prefill from autoregressive decoding and measure TTFT, TPOT, throughput and queue delay
Simulate admission and token-level scheduling under a concurrency bound and expose head-of-line blocking
Construct a load test that captures latency percentiles and KV-cache capacity rather than relying on average tokens/s
lessons.hook: A serving benchmark reports 3,000 output tokens per second, yet a customer waits ten seconds before the first token. Is the system fast or slow? Both statements may be true: throughput rewards batching while user experience depends on admission, prompt prefill and decode scheduling. This lesson examines the trade-off by implementing a deliberately simple scheduler and asking where it fails.
explanation: Language-model serving has two very different compute phases. During prefill the model processes all prompt tokens and materializes key/value states for attention. Prefill often contains substantial parallel matrix work. During autoregressive decode each active request produces one token step at a time while reusing cached keys and values. Depending on batch size, context length, model, and hardware, decoding can be more dependent on memory movement than prefill. The scheduler therefore has at least two scarce budgets: accelerator time and KV-cache residency. A single reported tokens-per-second number conceals which phase dominated, whether prompts were truncated, and whether requests waited in a queue. Measure time to first token (TTFT), time per output token (TPOT, ideally calculated per request), end-to-end latency and output tokens/s. Do not conflate TPOT and the reciprocal of aggregate throughput when multiple sequences are decoding concurrently.

Consider static batching: a server waits for a fixed set of requests, computes them together, and frees batch capacity only when the longest generation ends. Short generations may complete their mathematical work early but cannot always release slots. Continuous or iteration-level batching admits new requests as capacity becomes available between decode iterations. It improves utilization under varied request lengths, but an admission policy still faces difficult choices. A long-prompt request can stall tokens from existing short requests if prefills are scheduled without preemption. Priority queues can reduce latency for preferred users but starve low-priority traffic. Every scheduling comparison needs an explicit service-time model, admission rule and workload distribution; two schedulers with different admission policies are not comparable based on one contrived trace.

To model latency, let a request arrive at a_i, emit its first token at f_i, and complete at c_i. Then TTFT_i=f_i-a_i and end-to-end latency_i=c_i-a_i. Output throughput over observation interval [t0,t1] equals total emitted tokens divided by (t1-t0). Request throughput is completed requests divided by that interval and is not interchangeable with output token throughput. Report a warm-up interval, offered load, admitted requests, errors, timeouts and token distributions. Percentiles are computed over per-request latencies, not by taking a percentile of per-minute averages. Queueing theory gives a warning: as utilization approaches one, bursty arrivals can produce rapidly growing tail latency even when mean service capacity exceeds mean arrival rate. Little's law L=λW applies to a stable system with consistently defined population and time horizon; it is not an excuse to estimate user latency from a peak GPU kernel benchmark.

KV-cache storage couples scheduling to architecture. For a full resident cache under a simple contiguous assumption, bytes ≈ 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × cached tokens × concurrent requests × bytes per value. Sharing or paging changes allocation waste and may add metadata. PagedAttention uses block-based cache management to reduce fragmentation and enable sharing, but does not eliminate the actual key/value tensor data. An experienced serving engineer ends with a falsification benchmark. Load short and long prompts together, vary offered concurrency, record p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT, include cancelled requests and verify that completed token counts match emitted trace events. Under sustained overload, choose an explicit admission-control or backpressure policy rather than silently allowing unlimited queues. The toy simulator below treats prefill as an indivisible duration and decode steps as equally priced; it intentionally omits network overhead, parallel GPU execution and real kernel timing. Its value is to make admission assumptions inspectable, not to predict production latency. Replace its simple costs with measurement-based distributions before forecasting a deployment.

lessons.title: Quantization and Memory
objectives: Decompose inference memory into weights, quantization metadata, active KV cache and runtime overhead
Apply grouped symmetric quantization and compute reconstruction error and memory tradeoffs
Plan accuracy, throughput and latency evaluations separately for weight-only and weight-plus-activation quantization
lessons.hook: An 8-billion-parameter model is often described as an eight-gigabyte problem when converted to 8-bit weights. An engineer reserves eight gigabytes on a GPU and the service crashes during a long conversation. The model weights were only the starting line: cache residency, scales, workspace, activations and runtime buffers also consume memory. Quantization changes arithmetic representation and performance behavior; it does not repeal the laws of serving capacity.
explanation: Quantization maps values from a higher-precision representation to a lower-precision codebook, trading representational fidelity for compact storage and potentially more efficient arithmetic. For simple symmetric uniform quantization, a real value x is mapped to integer q=clip(round(x/s),qmin,qmax) and reconstructed as x̂=sq. Scale s may be assigned globally, per tensor, per output channel or per small block. Per-channel and group-wise scales can preserve small-valued channels beside large outliers but increase metadata storage and kernel bookkeeping. Asymmetric schemes use a zero-point; they are useful for skewed ranges but complicate arithmetic. Quantization error is not only absolute weight error: a slight perturbation in attention logits can change token probabilities, especially near competing output tokens. Different layer sensitivities justify mixed precision or excluding a few vulnerable layers from compression.

Weight-only quantization, written for example W4A16, keeps activations at a higher precision but compresses weights; the serving kernel typically dequantizes or multiplies using specialized instructions. W8A8 quantizes weights and activations, which can reduce memory movement and improve arithmetic on suitable hardware. Whether W4A16 is faster than W8A8 depends on microarchitecture, batch size, matrix dimensions, kernel availability, packing and dequantization overhead. Precision labels do not alone promise a speedup. For models with extremely low batch size, reducing weights moved from memory may dominate; for larger batches, matrix compute utilization and supported FP8 arithmetic may become decisive. Hardware support and numerical behavior must be checked for the exact accelerator and library version; a successful file conversion is not proof that the runtime uses an efficient low-bit kernel.

Weight bytes approximate P × b_w/8 for P parameters and b_w bits per parameter, ignoring padding. Metadata matters. If each group of g weights uses a 16-bit scale, scale overhead is roughly ceil(P/g) × 2 bytes, before any zero points or per-layer descriptor arrays. Example: seven billion parameters at 4 bits require 3.5 billion packed weight bytes plus approximately 109.375 million bytes of 16-bit scales with groups of 128. Convert decimal bytes to binary GiB carefully; 3.5 billion bytes is about 3.26 GiB. This still omits aligned storage and layer workspaces. A common planning failure is to quote 3.5 GB as the *total* deployment requirement, ignoring that the model may require separate BF16 embeddings, norms, a runtime graph and cache capacity for concurrent requests.

KV-cache memory should be separately estimated using 2 × L × Hkv × Dhead × T × B × bytes_per_cached_value. Here L is layers, Hkv is KV heads (not necessarily query heads), Dhead is head width, T is retained tokens per sequence, and B is concurrent sequences. For 32 layers, 8 KV heads, dimension 128, 4,096 tokens, two simultaneous sequences and 16-bit cache entries, the result is 1,073,741,824 bytes = 1024 MiB. Halving cache storage to 8-bit may roughly halve raw cache tensor bytes, but metadata, quantization scales, chunking and kernel requirements may alter actual allocation. In practice token length varies across users, prefix sharing matters, and cache paging can reduce fragmentation. Reserve the peak rather than mean context length when designing OOM-safe admission.

A robust post-training quantization evaluation has three independent axes. First, quality: task-specific exactness, calibration, long-context retrieval, multilingual behavior, adversarial inputs and output stability. Second, performance: per-request TTFT and TPOT as well as aggregate tokens/s across realistic batch sizes and prompt lengths. Third, reliability: OOM events, long-tail cache use, kernel fallbacks, numerical NaNs and deployment-version compatibility. Compare against an unquantized baseline at the same prompt and generation budgets; avoid claims derived from cherry-picked perplexity alone. Examine quality by slice because a small overall average loss can hide severe failures on rare formatting or numeric tasks. The Python code provides an intentionally educational symmetric quantizer and exact memory estimate. Production quantizers involve more sophisticated calibration, packing and supported kernels than this baseline.
